title: I tested 16 trading ideas across crypto, forex and commodities. 15 failed. The one that "worked" taught me the most.
author: Ok_Map5721
selftext:
Long post, sorry. I've been lurking here a while and figured I owe the sub something back.

Some background so you know where I'm coming from. I'm not a quant and I don't work at a fund. I built a crypto futures bot, got excited, and then slowly watched every assumption I had fall apart one by one. Along the way I ended up testing ideas on crypto, forex and commodities. Final score: 16 hypotheses, 15 rejected, and zero real money lost, which honestly is the only stat I'm proud of.

Here's what actually happened, in roughly the order it hurt.

\*\*The bot that couldn't find anything\*\*

First version had about 40 features, the usual stuff. EMAs, MACD, RSI style momentum, volatility, volume. Trained a model, backtested, looked decent. On the demo account it lost steadily. Win rate on closes was 22%.

So I made the rules honest. Real costs, a correction for how many things I was trying, and walk-forward testing where the model only ever sees data from before the trade. 224 candidate setups got evaluated across 7 retraining windows.

Zero passed.

The bot just stopped trading. At first I thought it was broken. It wasn't. It was the first time it was telling the truth.

\*\*The t-stat that wasn't\*\*

At one point I had a result with t = 16.9. If you don't do stats, that's basically "this is not luck, guaranteed." I was very happy for about a day.

Then I noticed I was predicting 12 hour returns but sampling every 5 minutes. So each row shared almost the whole future with the next one. I was counting the same price move over and over. After fixing it, t = 1.28. Nothing.

If you take one thing from this post: when your target window is longer than your bar, your rows are not independent and your stats are lying to you.

\*\*Six features that worked on random noise\*\*

Six of my features were fed in as raw price levels instead of normalized. Raw EMA values, raw OBV, that kind of thing. They "predicted" returns. So I tested them on a completely random walk, fake prices with no pattern at all. They still looked significant.

That was a fun afternoon. Run your features on noise before you run them on real data.

\*\*Forex: the pattern that died on the second pair\*\*

Forex costs are way lower than crypto, so I thought it'd be easier. EUR/USD hourly, 156 feature checks, nothing significant after correction. But splitting by hour of day, the London morning looked profitable on both halves of the data. Correlation between halves was 0.5. I got my hopes up again.

Before testing anything else I wrote down the exact rule and tested it on GBP/USD. It failed. The two pairs didn't even agree on direction. If I hadn't checked a second pair I'd probably be trading that today and wondering why it stopped working.

\*\*The part that changed how I see everything\*\*

This one's a bit nerdy but it's the most useful thing I learned.

I went back through all my "nothing found" results and asked a different question: could the test have found something even if it was there? For each one I calculated the smallest effect the test was able to detect.

7 out of 12 of my conclusions were worthless. The tests were blind. The smallest detectable effect was bigger than the trading costs, so they couldn't have seen a profitable strategy even if it was sitting right there. My commodity tests were blind on every single timeframe.

And here's the twist I didn't expect: the cheaper a market is to trade, the harder it is to test. Moving to forex and commodities for lower costs actually made my tests worse. Nobody told me that.

So now I don't trust any result, positive or negative, unless it says what it could and couldn't have detected.

\*\*The cost number I never checked\*\*

My whole crypto conclusion was based on round trip costs of 0.16%. Half of that was fees, confirmed. The other half was slippage, which I'd typed into a config file early on and never looked at again.

Tried measuring it on the exchange's testnet. Spread came back at 0.438%, which is insane, because testnet has no real market makers. Don't measure anything real on testnet.

Then I just polled the real order book for two hours. No account, no trading. Spread sat at one tick the entire time. Actual slippage was 5.5x lower than what I'd assumed.

So the costs were wrong, and wrong against me. Which brought one mean reversion signal back from "hopeless" to "maybe."

\*\*The "maybe" that wasn't\*\*

I reran it on fresh data and the effect showed up again, almost the same size. Real effect, not a fluke. Great.

Except the noise per trade was 13 times bigger than the signal. Once I accounted for how many things I'd tried along the way, the math said I'd need something like 18,000 independent trades to prove it's real. Years and years of data.

So it exists, probably, and I still can't trade it. That one stung more than the clear failures.

\*\*What I'd tell myself at the start\*\*

\- A beautiful backtest is a warning sign, not a result  
\- Measure your costs, don't type them in  
\- Count every version you tried, including the ones you deleted  
\- Check if your test could even see what you're looking for  
\- Test your pipeline on random data first  
\- A bot that refuses to trade might be the smartest bot you've built

I'm not saying nobody has an edge. I'm saying almost everything that looks like one isn't, and the tools to find out are boring and cheap.

Happy to answer questions in the comments, especially if you're about to make one of these mistakes. I've made all of them.

comments.author: Tradenoss
comments.body: Keeping the 15 rejected ideas in the write-up is the most useful part of this. Plenty of people would have loosened the filter until something passed. Since you already corrected for the number of tries, a small forward test on data the survivor has never seen is the next fair check.

replies.author: Ok_Map5721
replies.body:
Thanks, and yeah, loosening the filter until something passes is exactly how most of the backtests posted here get made.

On the forward test, I thought the same at first. The problem is the size of the thing. The noise per trade is about 13x the signal, so a few months of forward data would come back looking like a coin flip whether the effect is real or not. You'd need thousands of independent trades before the result means anything, and by then the market has probably changed anyway.

That was the hardest lesson for me: a forward test only helps if the effect is big enough for the test to see. Otherwise it just gives you a fresh random number to get attached to.

replies.author: Tradenoss
replies.body: fair, the 13x number makes that concrete. if the effect is that small, a forward test mostly checks the plumbing: costs, fills, and that the live code does what the backtest code did. still worth knowing before any money goes in, but it won't prove the edge

replies.author: Ok_Map5721
replies.body:
Exactly, that's the right way to think about it. Plumbing check, not proof.

The plumbing bit actually bit me before any forward test. My first backtester was separate code from the live bot, and they quietly drifted apart. Entries in the backtest filled at the signal bar's close, the live bot could only act on the next bar's open. Small difference on paper, big one in results.

What fixed it was rewriting the backtester to call the bot's own selection and execution functions directly. Same code path for both, so they literally can't disagree. Probably the most useful refactor I did in the whole project.

replies.author: Tradenoss
replies.body: same code path is the right fix. signal-bar close vs next-bar open looks like a rounding error on paper and then quietly eats the edge. did fees and slippage go through those same functions too, or were they still modelled on the side?

comments.author: LipTicklers
comments.body: “I have no idea what im doing but im going to post about it anyway”

replies.author: Ok_Map5721
replies.body:
Fair enough, I get why it reads that way. But the post is the opposite: every one of those ideas got tested properly and closed, and I wrote it up so people don't burn months repeating the same mistakes I made.

What I'm working on now I won't post, for two reasons. It's not proven yet, and if it ever is, nobody in their right mind puts a working edge on Reddit. Publishing an alpha is the fastest way to kill it.

So what you get here is the graveyard. Still useful, I think.

comments.author: Signal_Pace_7968
comments.body:
Good write up. The “could the test even see it” part is the one almost nobody does.

I ran into the same thing comparing rules against random entries in the same stock with the same exits. A rule with 30 trades can look better than 90% of the random versions and still be noise, because the trades often sit in the same few weeks and move together.

How did you handle that for the minimum detectable effect? Did you count overlapping trades as one, or use something like block bootstrap?

replies.author: Ok_Map5721
replies.body:
Thanks. Simpler than block bootstrap: I counted effective independent observations, roughly N divided by the holding horizon in bars, so overlapping trades collapse into one. The minimum detectable effect came from that number and the per-trade volatility, at 5% significance and 80% power.

It's crude but it's brutal in the right direction. One of my cross-sectional tests looked like hundreds of data points and turned out to have 34 independent observations, which put the detection threshold above 5%. Nothing real at that size, so the test was blind.

Your point about trades bunching in the same few weeks is the one I handled worst. Counting by horizon fixes overlap in time, but not regime clustering, where separate trades are all riding the same move. Block bootstrap would catch more of that. Honestly, my numbers are probably still a bit optimistic there.

comments.author: trunksta
comments.body: T stat of 16 was the red flag that you had some kind of major lookahead issue

replies.author: Ok_Map5721
replies.body: Close, but it wasn't lookahead, which surprised me too. The features only used past data. The problem was the target: 12-hour forward returns sampled every 5 minutes, so neighbouring rows shared almost the same future and the test counted one move a hundred-plus times. Same symptom as lookahead, a t-stat way too good to be true, different cause. Fixing the sampling took it to 1.28.

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body: Counting the failed ideas and checking whether your tests could even detect an edge is the part most people skip. The lesson about overlapping rows is a good one, since a long target window on short bars makes the stats look far stronger than they are. One thing I'd add is writing the rule and the test before looking at any result, so the count of tries stays honest. Cymetica's Backtest Labs has a fee setting and a held out stretch of data, which supports that kind of discipline.

replies.author: Ok_Map5721
replies.body:
Agreed, that's the one that saved me in forex. EUR/USD showed the London morning hours as profitable on both halves of the data, and I was this close to believing it. Instead I wrote the exact rule down first, which hours, which direction, what counts as a pass, and only then ran it on GBP/USD. It failed cleanly.

Without writing it down, I know exactly what I'd have done: "well, GBP is a different pair, let's shift the window an hour." And then another hour. That's how one honest test quietly becomes twenty.

Fees and a held-out stretch help, but no tool fixes it if you peek at the holdout and then tweak. It only works if you touch it once.
